extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, poets, and educated readers interested in poetic theory and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating poetry and the conduct of reviewers, including standards for fair criticism, distinguishing imagination from fancy, and criteria for poetic excellence (style, diction, metre, atmosphere, moral content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground reviews on fixed canons deduced from human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Till reviews are conducted on far other principles, and with far other motives; till in the place of arbitrary dictation and petulant sneers, the reviewers support their decisions by reference to fixed canons of criticism, previously established and deduced from the nature of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should justify judgments by appeal to established critical principles (derived from human nature and the arts), not by whim, personal malice, or transient taste. Anti-pattern: arbitrary dictation, petulant sneers, or purely personal invective without principled basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize elucidation of beauties over merely pointing out defects
rubrics_metrics.description: He, who points out and elucidates the beauties of an original work does indeed give me interesting information; he who tells me that there are defects in a new work, tells me nothing which I should not have taken for granted without his information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful critic adds value by explicating and illuminating a work's merits and why they matter. Merely cataloguing defects is of little informational value to a reader who can notice those defects unaided. Good criticism should teach appreciation as well as identify faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by characteristic qualities, not by accidental failures
rubrics_metrics.description: I know nothing that surpasses the vileness of deciding on the merits of a poet or painter ... by accidental failures or faulty passages; except the impudence of defending it, as the proper duty, and most instructive part, of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should focus on characteristic strengths and defects that reveal an artist's true quality. Anti-pattern: seizing isolated bad lines or failures (e.g., minor background details in a painting) and treating them as representative of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate collections holistically; minor or playful pieces should not define reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The merest trifle he ever sent abroad had tenfold better claims to its ink and paper than all the silly criticisms on it ... In the Lyrical Ballads ... the lines and passages which might have offended the general taste, would have been considered as mere inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a volume, distinguish substantial core works from minor, playful, or experimental pieces. Minor poems that might be 'passed over' should not be used to discredit the entire collection. Consider omission or contextualizing of a few lines when assessing overall merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply consistent standards to living and deceased authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Why should we judge by a different rule two printed works, only because the one author is alive, and the other in his grave?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same criteria of merit and fault should be used regardless of the author's life status. Anti-pattern: granting indulgence to dead authors while disparaging living ones (or vice versa) for the same features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit occasional light or playful compositions if they are not immoral
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Southey was quite unable to comprehend, wherein could consist the crime or mischief of printing half a dozen or more playful poems ... provided they contained nothing immoral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may publish occasional, slight, or playful pieces without it damaging their reputation provided such pieces are morally unobjectionable. These works can demonstrate versatility and add to an author's honour rather than diminish it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid amplifying trivial defects by reprinting them as representative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If in a volume of poetry the critic should find poem or passage which he deems more especially worthless, he is sure to select and reprint it in the review; by which ... he wastes as much more paper than the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not magnify a work's faults by reproducing them widely as if representative. Reprinting isolated bad passages (which reviews reach a much larger audience than the original) creates a distorted view and is unfair. Anti-pattern: quoting the worst lines at length and using them to define the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish imagination (higher) from fancy (lower)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy and Imagination were two distinct and widely different faculties ... To the faculty by which I had characterized Milton, we should confine the term 'imagination;' while the other would be contra-distinguished as 'fancy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and poets should recognize two different creative powers: imagination (transformative, synthesizing, idealizing, linked to profound thought and feeling) and fancy (associative, decorative, and often superficial). Correctly identifying which faculty is at work helps in appraisal and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic excellence: union of deep feeling with profound thought, and creation of atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: It was the union of deep feeling with profound thought; the fine balance of truth in observing, with the imaginative faculty in modifying, the objects observed; and above all the original gift of spreading the tone, the atmosphere, and with it the depth and height of the ideal world around forms, incidents, and situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry for its synthesis of feeling and thought, truthful observation transformed by imagination, and capacity to create a sustained tone or atmosphere that yields an 'ideal world' around subjects. Examples cited: Tintern Abbey, Lines on revisiting the Wye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of diction and metre; avoid prosaic words in feeble metre unless intentional
rubrics_metrics.description: The seductive faults ... prosaic words in feeble metre, silly thoughts in childish phrases, and a preference of mean, degrading, or at best trivial associations and characters ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction and metre must suit poetic aims; prosaic language and weak metre undermine poetic effect unless they are an intentional, artful simplicity serving the poem's purpose. Critics should judge whether plainness is a deliberate artistic choice or a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and control over language to avoid obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: The occasional obscurities, which had risen from an imperfect control over the resources of his native language, had almost wholly disappeared ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscurity in early work is often due to imperfect command of language. Good poetry displays sufficient control over diction and structure to avoid unnecessary obscurity; repeated attention and refinement can remove such faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form influences diction and allowable colloquial descent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spenserian stanza, which always, more or less, recalls to the reader’s mind Spenser’s own style, would doubtless have authorized ... a more frequent descent to the phrases of ordinary life, than could without an ill effect have been hazarded in the heroic couplet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose forms (stanza, metre) with awareness of their historical and stylistic associations; certain stanza-forms may permit more colloquial or ordinary phrasing without loss, whereas stricter forms demand elevated diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess authorial merit also by industry, range of acquirements, and moral character
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on the variety and extent of his acquirements! He stands second to no man, either as an historian or as a bibliographer ... His prose is always intelligible and always entertaining ... his matchless industry and perseverance ... his generous submission to tasks of transitory interest ... having thus more than satisfied the claims of affection or prudence, he should yet have made for himself time and power, to achieve more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical and moral virtues (industry, perseverance, breadth of learning, consistency of conduct) are relevant to a rounded evaluation of a writer's worth. These traits can inform judgments about reliability, seriousness of purpose, and the value of an author's corpus.
